blocks.text: Say you are fitting a line through a pile of house prices, running a search engine that ranks pages by similarity, or training a neural network that has millions of weights sitting in a handful of matrices. Underneath every one of those jobs is the same small set of operations: multiplying matrices together, solving for an unknown vector, finding the directions along which data stretches the most. NumPy bundles all of that into one submodule, numpy.linalg, and this lesson walks through exactly what lives in it and why each piece matters.
1. Introduction

You already know how to build arrays, reshape them, and run elementwise math on them from earlier lessons in this module. Linear algebra is a different animal. Instead of treating every number independently, it treats whole rows and columns as single mathematical objects, vectors and matrices, and asks questions like: what happens when this matrix acts on that vector, can this system of equations be solved, and which directions in the data matter most. Those are exactly the questions numpy.linalg answers.

blocks.caption: The four families of tools this lesson covers, all living inside numpy.linalg.

blocks.text: A quick map of what is ahead. You will see proper matrix multiplication and how it differs from the elementwise star operator you already know. You will learn why inverting a matrix by hand is usually the wrong move, and what to do instead. You will see determinants, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, singular value decomposition, and matrix norms, each tied back to something you will actually run into building machine learning systems.

blocks.text: 2. Matrix Multiplication Done Properly

Neural network layers, attention scores in a transformer, the forward pass of basically every model you will train, all of it comes down to multiplying matrices together in the proper mathematical sense. NumPy gives you two equivalent ways to do this, and getting comfortable with them is non negotiable if you plan to write any ML code.
2.1 The @ Operator and np.matmul

True matrix multiplication takes the rows of the first matrix and the columns of the second, multiplies matching entries together, and sums them up, one sum per output cell. NumPy exposes this through np.matmul and, more conveniently, through the @ operator, which does exactly the same thing with far less typing.

code.content:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[1, 2],
              [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6],
              [7, 8]])

C = A @ B            # same as np.matmul(A, B)
print(C)
# [[19 22]
#  [43 50]]

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing rows of matrix A and columns of matrix B feeding into row times column sums, producing a result matrix
blocks.caption: Matrix multiplication combines a whole row with a whole column to produce each output cell.

blocks.text: For this to even be defined, the number of columns in the first matrix has to match the number of rows in the second. Mismatch that and NumPy raises a shape error immediately rather than guessing what you meant, which is exactly the behavior you want from something this fundamental.
2.2 Why This Is Not Elementwise Multiplication

The mathematical operations lesson already walked through the contrast between elementwise multiplication and matrix multiplication in some depth, so this is just a reminder of the headline fact, because it is easy to forget under pressure. The plain * operator between two arrays always multiplies matching positions independently. It has nothing to do with rows meeting columns.

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing array A position i and array B position i multiplying independently into a result of the same shape
blocks.caption: Elementwise multiply never lets one position touch another. Matrix multiply is built entirely on that mixing.

code.content:
A * B
# [[ 5 12]
#  [21 32]]   elementwise, position by position

A @ B
# [[19 22]
#  [43 50]]   real matrix multiplication

blocks.title: The single most common NumPy bug
blocks.content: Writing A * B when you meant A @ B will not throw an error if the shapes happen to line up, it will just silently give you the wrong numbers. This is one of the sneakiest bugs in machine learning code, because the script keeps running, the loss just never quite makes sense. Whenever two matrices are being combined and you mean real matrix multiplication, reach for @ or np.matmul, never the plain star.

blocks.text: 2.3 Batched Matrix Multiplication

Real training code almost never multiplies just one pair of matrices at a time. You usually have a whole batch of examples, stored as a 3D array shaped like batch size, rows, columns. The good news is that @ and np.matmul understand this automatically. When you feed them 3D arrays, they treat the first axis as a batch dimension and run ordinary matrix multiplication independently on each pair of 2D slices.

code.content:
batch_X = np.random.randn(32, 4, 6)   # 32 matrices, each 4 by 6
batch_W = np.random.randn(32, 6, 3)   # 32 matrices, each 6 by 3

out = batch_X @ batch_W
print(out.shape)   # (32, 4, 3), one 4 by 3 result per item in the batch

blocks.text: This is exactly the mechanism transformer attention leans on: every sequence in a batch gets its own query, key, and value matrices multiplied together, all in one vectorized call instead of a Python loop over the batch. It is the same rule you already know from broadcasting, applied to the last two axes while the leading axes get matched up like a batch.
3. The Dot Products Double Life

np.dot is the function that trips people up the most in this entire module, because it quietly does two completely different things depending on what you hand it. Understanding this overload cold will save you real debugging time later.
3.1 Two Vectors In, One Scalar Out

When both inputs are plain 1D vectors, np.dot multiplies matching positions together and adds up the results into a single number. This is the classic dot product from geometry class, and it shows up constantly in machine learning, for example computing the raw score of one neuron before an activation function is applied.

code.content:
u = np.array([1, 2, 3])
v = np.array([4, 5, 6])

score = np.dot(u, v)
print(score)   # 32, a single scalar
# 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing vector u and vector v feeding into np dot, producing a single scalar
blocks.caption: Feed np.dot two 1D vectors and you always get back exactly one number.

blocks.text: 3.2 Two Matrices In, One Matrix Out

Hand np.dot two 2D arrays instead, and it stops behaving like the vector dot product entirely. It switches over to ordinary matrix multiplication, the same operation you just saw with @, and hands you back a full matrix, not a single number.

code.content:
X = np.array([[1, 2],
              [3, 4]])
Y = np.array([[5, 6],
              [7, 8]])

result = np.dot(X, Y)
print(result)
# [[19 22]
#  [43 50]]   a matrix, not a scalar

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing matrix X and matrix Y feeding into np dot, producing a result matrix rather than a scalar
blocks.caption: The exact same function name, np.dot, now returns a full matrix once both inputs are 2D.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Inputs","np.dot behavior","np.matmul or @ behavior"],"rows":[["Two 1D vectors","Scalar, the classic dot product","Not allowed, matmul refuses plain scalars from two 1D vectors the same way"],["Two 2D matrices","Matrix product, identical to matmul","Matrix product, identical to dot"],["3D batched arrays","Does not broadcast over batches the way you would expect","Broadcasts over the leading batch dimension correctly"]]}

blocks.title: Pick matmul for matrices, on purpose
blocks.content: Because np.dot changes behavior based on input shape, and does not broadcast batches the sensible way, most experienced NumPy users reserve np.dot for genuine 1D vector dot products and use @ or np.matmul for anything 2D or higher. It removes an entire category of shape surprises from your code.

blocks.text: 4. Transpose, Briefly Revisited

The reshaping lesson already covered .T in full detail, including exactly why it is a relabeling of strides rather than a real copy. In the linear algebra world, the transpose shows up constantly for a much simpler reason: a huge number of formulas are written in terms of a matrix and its own transpose. You will see this everywhere from computing a covariance matrix to solving the normal equation later in this lesson, so it is worth having .T fresh in your mind as you read on.

code.content:
X = np.array([[1, 2],
              [3, 4],
              [5, 6]])

XtX = X.T @ X
print(XtX.shape)   # (2, 2), a square matrix built entirely from X and its transpose

blocks.text: 5. Solving Linear Systems the Right Way

A huge amount of classical machine learning boils down to solving an equation of the form A x equals b for the unknown vector x. Linear regression, some optimization steps, plenty of engineering simulations, they all reduce to this exact shape of problem. NumPy gives you two ways to approach it, and only one of them is usually the right call.
5.1 What np.linalg.inv Actually Computes

np.linalg.inv computes the inverse of a square matrix, the matrix that, when multiplied by the original, gives you back the identity matrix. Once you have that inverse, solving A x equals b looks tempting: just multiply both sides by the inverse of A, and x falls out.

code.content:
A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0],
              [1.0, 3.0]])
b = np.array([3.0, 5.0])

A_inv = np.linalg.inv(A)
x = A_inv @ b
print(x)   # [0.8 1.4]

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing matrix A leading to computing its inverse, then multiplying the inverse by vector b, arriving at solution x
blocks.caption: The tempting but roundabout path: compute a full inverse first, then use it to reach x.

blocks.text: 5.2 Prefer np.linalg.solve Over Explicit Inversion

Here is the part that surprises people coming from a pure math background. Explicitly computing a matrix inverse is slower than it needs to be, and worse, it is numerically less stable, meaning small rounding errors already present in your data can get amplified into much bigger errors in the answer. NumPy has a dedicated function, np.linalg.solve, that finds x directly without ever forming the inverse as an intermediate step, and it is both faster and more accurate.

code.content:
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)   # [0.8 1.4], same answer, computed more directly and more safely

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing matrix A and vector b feeding directly into np linalg solve, arriving at solution x, marked as the preferred path
blocks.caption: The direct path: solve reaches x in one stable step, without ever forming a full inverse.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","np.linalg.inv then multiply","np.linalg.solve"],"rows":[["Speed on larger matrices","Slower, does strictly more work","Faster, skips the unnecessary inverse"],["Numerical stability","Can amplify rounding error","Generally more stable"],["What you actually need most of the time","A full inverse, rarely needed on its own","Just the solution vector x, which is usually the actual goal"],["Recommendation","Use only when you truly need the inverse itself","Prefer this whenever the goal is solving A x equals b"]]}

blocks.title: Reach for solve by default
blocks.content: If your end goal is a vector x that satisfies A x equals b, whether that is a linear regression coefficient or a physics simulation, call np.linalg.solve directly. Only reach for np.linalg.inv when you genuinely need the inverse matrix itself for some other calculation, not just as a stepping stone.

blocks.text: 6. Determinants and Singular Matrices

The determinant is a single number computed from a square matrix, and np.linalg.det hands it to you directly. What matters most for practical work is not the formula behind it but what the value tells you: a matrix whose determinant is exactly zero has no inverse at all. Mathematicians call this a singular matrix, meaning at least one row can be written as a combination of the others, so the matrix throws away information rather than preserving it.

code.content:
singular = np.array([[1, 2],
                      [2, 4]])   # second row is just the first row doubled

print(np.linalg.det(singular))   # 0.0

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing matrix A leading to a determinant of zero, leading to no inverse existing, leading to rows being dependent
blocks.caption: A zero determinant is not an edge case to shrug off, it means the matrix genuinely cannot be inverted.

blocks.text: In practice you will rarely see an exact zero. Floating point arithmetic almost never lands precisely on zero, so what you actually see is a determinant that is extremely close to zero relative to the size of the matrix entries. That near zero value is called an ill conditioned matrix, and it deserves the same caution as an exactly singular one, because computations involving it, including calling np.linalg.inv on it, become unreliable long before the determinant technically reaches zero.

blocks.alt: A small diagram contrasting a well conditioned matrix leading to stable computation with a near singular matrix leading to unstable computation
blocks.caption: How close a matrix sits to singular directly predicts how much you should trust computations built on it.

blocks.title: Check before you invert
blocks.content: If you are about to call np.linalg.inv or np.linalg.solve on a matrix you are unsure about, a quick np.linalg.det check, or better, inspecting np.linalg.cond, can warn you before you trust an answer that is secretly built on shaky numerical ground.

blocks.text: 7. Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors, and PCA

Most vectors, when you multiply them by a matrix, end up pointing in some new direction entirely. Eigenvectors are the special exceptions: multiply an eigenvector by its matrix and it comes out pointing the exact same direction it started in, just stretched or shrunk by some factor. That stretching factor is the eigenvalue. np.linalg.eig finds both at once for a square matrix.
7.1 What np.linalg.eig Returns

code.content:
A = np.array([[2.0, 0.0],
              [0.0, 3.0]])

eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(eigenvalues)    # [2. 3.]
print(eigenvectors)
# [[1. 0.]
#  [0. 1.]]   each column is one eigenvector

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing vector v multiplied by matrix A resulting in the same direction stretched, labeled with eigenvalue lambda
blocks.caption: An eigenvector keeps its own direction after being multiplied by the matrix, it just gets scaled by the eigenvalue.

blocks.text: Notice the function returns two things at once, a 1D array of eigenvalues and a 2D array whose columns are the matching eigenvectors. It is easy to accidentally index into the wrong axis here, so always double check with .shape the first time you use it on a new matrix.
7.2 PCA Is an Eigendecomposition

Principal component analysis, one of the most widely used dimensionality reduction techniques in machine learning, is fundamentally nothing more than an eigendecomposition applied to a covariance matrix. You compute the covariance matrix of your features, find its eigenvectors, and those eigenvectors are exactly the principal components, the directions along which your data spreads out the most. The matching eigenvalues tell you how much variance each direction actually captures.

code.content:
data = np.random.randn(200, 3)              # 200 samples, 3 features
cov = np.cov(data, rowvar=False)            # 3 by 3 covariance matrix

eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(cov)
order = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1]       # largest variance first
principal_components = eigenvectors[:, order]

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing a data matrix leading to a covariance matrix, leading to eigenvectors and eigenvalues, leading to principal components
blocks.caption: PCA in one sentence: eigendecompose the covariance matrix, and the eigenvectors are your new axes.

blocks.title: Why this matters beyond the math class definition
blocks.content: The next time someone describes PCA as mysterious dimensionality reduction magic, you can point directly at this: it is sorting the eigenvalues of a covariance matrix from largest to smallest and keeping the eigenvectors attached to the biggest ones. Nothing more exotic than that.

blocks.text: 8. Singular Value Decomposition, a Sturdier Alternative

Eigendecomposition has a real limitation: it is only defined for square matrices, and it can behave poorly numerically even then. Singular value decomposition, computed with np.linalg.svd, generalizes the same idea, breaking down data by its dominant directions, to any matrix shape at all, and it does so with noticeably better numerical stability. This is exactly why production PCA implementations, including the one inside scikit learn, actually run SVD under the hood rather than calling eig directly on a covariance matrix.

code.content:
data_centered = data - data.mean(axis=0)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(data_centered, full_matrices=False)

print(S.shape)    # (3,), the singular values, largest first
print(Vt.shape)   # (3, 3), rows of Vt are the same principal directions PCA wants

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing matrix A of any shape decomposing into U Sigma V transpose, which works for non square matrices and is more numerically stable
blocks.caption: SVD does everything eigendecomposition does for covariance matrices, but works on any shape and holds up better numerically.

blocks.text: You do not need to memorize the internals of U, the singular values in S, and Vt to use this productively. The practical takeaway is simpler: whenever a library or algorithm needs to find the dominant directions in a batch of data, and it needs to do that reliably at scale, reach for or trust SVD over a raw eigendecomposition.
9. Matrix Norms and Vector Magnitude

Sometimes you do not care about the direction of a vector at all, you just want one number describing how big it is. That is exactly what np.linalg.norm gives you, and it shows up constantly in training loops, loss functions, and regularization terms.
9.1 Measuring How Big a Vector Is

code.content:
v = np.array([3.0, 4.0])
print(np.linalg.norm(v))   # 5.0, the familiar straight line length

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing vector v feeding into np linalg norm, producing a single length value
blocks.caption: The norm collapses an entire vector down into one number describing its overall size.

blocks.content: {"headers":["ord parameter","What it measures","Common name"],"rows":[["1","Sum of absolute values of every entry","L1 norm, also called Manhattan distance from the origin"],["2, the default","Straight line distance from the origin","L2 norm, also called Euclidean norm"],["np.inf","The single largest absolute value among the entries","Max norm or infinity norm"]]}

blocks.text: 9.2 Gradient Clipping and Regularization

During training, gradients can occasionally explode into enormous values, which sends the model weights flying off into nonsense. Gradient clipping is the standard fix, and it works by measuring the norm of the gradient vector and rescaling it down whenever that norm crosses some threshold you pick ahead of time.

code.content:
def clip_gradient(grad, max_norm=5.0):
    norm = np.linalg.norm(grad)
    if norm > max_norm:
        grad = grad * (max_norm / norm)
    return grad

exploded = np.array([40.0, 30.0])   # norm is 50
clipped = clip_gradient(exploded)
print(np.linalg.norm(clipped))      # 5.0, direction kept, size reined in

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing a gradient vector having its norm computed, then branching into rescale gradient if the norm is above a threshold, or keep as is otherwise
blocks.caption: Gradient clipping never changes direction, it only shrinks magnitude once the norm crosses a limit.

blocks.title: Norms show up in regularization too
blocks.content: L2 regularization, the penalty term that discourages a model from leaning on any single weight too heavily, is nothing more than adding the norm of the weight vector, squared, into the loss function. The same np.linalg.norm you just used for gradient clipping is doing double duty here.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example, the Normal Equation

Time to put several pieces from this lesson together at once. Linear regression has a closed form solution called the normal equation, which finds the best fit weights w directly, without any gradient descent loop, by solving w equals the inverse of X transpose X, all multiplied by X transpose y. You already know enough now to see exactly why that inverse should never actually be computed explicitly.

code.content:
np.random.seed(0)
X = np.random.randn(100, 3)              # 100 samples, 3 features
true_w = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5])
y = X @ true_w + np.random.randn(100) * 0.1   # noisy targets

X_design = np.hstack([X, np.ones((100, 1))])  # add a bias column

blocks.alt: A small diagram showing X transpose X and X transpose y both feeding into np linalg solve, producing the weights w
blocks.caption: The whole normal equation pipeline, built entirely on transpose, matrix multiply, and solve.

code.content:
XtX = X_design.T @ X_design
Xty = X_design.T @ y

w = np.linalg.solve(XtX, Xty)
print(w)   # close to [2.0, -1.0, 0.5, 0.0]

blocks.title: Never write np.linalg.inv(XtX) @ Xty in real code
blocks.content: It gives the same answer on well behaved data, but it does strictly more work and is more fragile the moment your features are even mildly correlated with each other, which real world data almost always is to some degree. np.linalg.solve is the version you want in production, and now you know exactly why.

blocks.text: 11. Wrapping Up

items: Use @ or np.matmul for real matrix multiplication, never the plain * operator, which always stays elementwise.
np.dot returns a scalar for two 1D vectors but a full matrix for two 2D arrays, the same function name hiding two different operations.
Prefer np.linalg.solve over np.linalg.inv whenever your actual goal is solving A x equals b, it is faster and more numerically stable.
A zero or near zero determinant from np.linalg.det means the matrix is singular or close to it, treat any computation built on it with suspicion.
np.linalg.eig gives you eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and PCA is nothing more than this decomposition applied to a covariance matrix.
np.linalg.svd generalizes the same idea to any matrix shape, more stably, and is what production PCA implementations actually run under the hood.
np.linalg.norm measures vector magnitude, and it powers both gradient clipping and L2 regularization in everyday training code.

blocks.title: The one habit worth keeping
blocks.content: Whenever you catch yourself about to explicitly invert a matrix, pause and ask whether you actually need the inverse itself, or whether you just need to solve a system. Nine times out of ten in machine learning work, it is the second one, and np.linalg.solve is sitting right there waiting for you.
